title: Vitamins and Scurvy
objective: After this level you can explain why vitamins matter, using scurvy as the example.
summary: Without vitamin C the body can't make collagen properly, and scurvy follows. James Lind saw citrus work in 1747, but blamed scurvy on digestion and damp air; the Navy acted in 1795.

cards.headline: In 1747, a ship's surgeon saw citrus beat scurvy. The Navy acted 48 years later.
cards.body: It's often told as a quick triumph: a doctor tries lemons, sailors are saved. The real story is slower, and more interesting. First, what was scurvy doing to those sailors?

cards.headline: The missing ingredient
cards.body: Scurvy is what happens without enough vitamin C. Your body needs it to make collagen, the protein that holds skin, blood vessels, bones and cartilage together. Without it, connective tissue weakens: tiredness, aching joints, swollen and bleeding gums, loose teeth, wounds that won't heal. Signs can appear within about a month, and untreated scurvy can kill. Many animals make their own vitamin C. Humans can't; we lack a working enzyme to do it.

events.label: On HMS Salisbury, James Lind gives 12 sailors with scurvy six remedies, two men each
The pair given oranges and lemons recover fastest; one is fit for duty within about six days
Lind's Treatise of the Scurvy reports the trial, without naming citrus the cure
The Royal Navy makes lemon juice standard issue
Vitamin C is identified as the factor that prevents scurvy

cards.headline: Why the lesson took 48 years
cards.body: Lind's comparison is seen as an early controlled clinical trial, but he didn't draw the lesson we see in it. He blamed scurvy mainly on damp air and a coarse diet the body failed to digest, not on a missing nutrient. He later recommended rob, a juice concentrate made by heating, and heat destroys vitamin C. The Admiralty adopted lemon juice in 1795, persuaded by Gilbert Blane. The evidence came early; the explanation came much later.

mascot.line: A good experiment can still be misread by the person who ran it. Science keeps checking.
